# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Finance Committee, Riverbend Community Health Center Board of Directors
**From:** Amara Osei, Director, Diabetes Management Program
**Date:** July 29, 2026
**Re:** Program Year 2024 Results and Renewal Options Ahead of Grant Expiration

---

## Purpose

The state grant supporting our diabetes management program expires in June. The committee has asked me to lay out what the program accomplished, what the data show, and what each of the three paths under consideration — renewal at current staffing, expansion to Milford, or wind-down — would cost. This memo is intended to give you what you need to make that call. I am not asking for a decision today, but I am asking that one be made in time to give staff and patients adequate notice.

## What the Program Did

We enrolled 412 patients in 2024. Each enrollee received an initial assessment, a personalized care plan, and a schedule of follow-up visits over twelve months, with nutrition counseling layered in where indicated. The work was carried by two full-time nurse educators and one part-time dietitian.

That staffing level is the central operational fact of the year. Two nurse educators managing 412 enrollees works out to roughly 206 patients each. The dietitian, at half-time, was the constraint on nutrition counseling throughout; we triaged access to her by clinical need rather than offering it to everyone who would have benefited.

## What the Numbers Show

**Retention.** Of 412 enrolled, 268 reached the twelve-month mark — a retention rate of 65 percent. That figure deserves the committee's attention in both directions. It is respectable for a program of this type, and it means two-thirds of the people who walked in the door stayed for a full year of structured care. It also means 144 patients did not. I do not currently have a rigorous accounting of why they left. Some moved, some lost coverage, some disengaged. Without exit data we are guessing, and I would flag that as a gap worth closing regardless of which option the committee chooses.

**Clinical results.** Average HbA1c among completers fell from 9.1 to 7.8 — a drop of 1.3 percentage points. This is a meaningful clinical result. A reduction of that size is associated with materially lower risk of retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy over time, and it moves a population from poorly controlled toward the general target range.

Two caveats belong in the record. First, this figure describes completers only. We do not know how the 144 who left fared, and it is reasonable to assume the group that stayed was more engaged than the group that did not. The true program-wide effect is almost certainly smaller than 1.3 points. Second, we have no control group. Some portion of this improvement would likely have occurred through ordinary primary care. I believe the program drove most of it, but I cannot prove that from these numbers alone.

What I can say with confidence is that 268 patients with poorly controlled diabetes ended the year substantially better controlled than they started it.

## The Three Options

**Option One: Renew at current staffing.** This holds two nurse educators and a half-time dietitian at Dover, serving roughly 400 patients annually. Cost is comparable to the current $185,000 grant level, adjusted for salary and benefit increases — I would budget in the range of $190,000 to $200,000 for a full year. This is the lowest-risk path. It preserves a functioning program and a trained staff. It does not address the retention gap or the dietitian bottleneck.

**Option Two: Expand to Milford.** Serving the Milford satellite would require at minimum one additional nurse educator and an increase in the dietitian's hours, plus travel, space, and materials. My working estimate is an additional $95,000 to $115,000 annually, bringing total program cost to roughly $285,000 to $315,000. That is a real number and I want the committee to see it plainly: expansion is not a marginal add-on. There is genuine unmet need in the Milford service area, and the model is proven. But expanding a program whose retention we do not yet understand risks scaling a weakness along with a strength.

**Option Three: Wind down.** This is the cheapest option on paper and the most expensive in practice. Current enrollees would need transition plans and referrals back to primary care, which is itself a cost in staff time over several months. We would lose two trained nurse educators who would be difficult and expensive to replace. And roughly 400 patients a year would lose access to structured diabetes management in a service area that has no comparable alternative. I do not recommend this path, but the committee is entitled to see it costed honestly rather than dismissed.

## What the Committee Needs to Decide

Three things, in this order.

**First, whether there is institutional appetite to continue the program without state funding, or with reduced state funding.** Everything else depends on this. If the answer is that the program lives or dies with the grant, our energy belongs in renewal applications and alternative funders, and I need direction on that now.

**Second, what evidence the committee would require to approve expansion.** If Milford is genuinely on the table, tell me what would satisfy you — retention analysis, cost-per-patient benchmarks, a needs assessment for the Milford catchment. I can produce those. I cannot produce them in the two months before a June deadline if the request comes in May.

**Third, the notice period.** If wind-down is a serious possibility, staff and patients need lead time. Ninety days is the minimum I would consider defensible for patients with chronic conditions who have built care relationships with our educators.

## Recommendation and Next Steps

My recommendation is renewal at current staffing for one additional year, paired with a focused effort to understand and improve retention, and a formal feasibility assessment for Milford to be delivered to this committee within six months. That path preserves what works, closes the most important gap in our evidence, and keeps expansion available as a decision made on data rather than optimism.

I can provide detailed line-item budgets for any of the three options within two weeks of the committee's request, and I am available to attend the next meeting to discuss.
